claim: MKLP2 is a kinesin-6 family motor involved at several key stages of cell division and is essential for cytokinesis in mammals.
source: MKLP2 (Kif20A), a kinesin-6 family motor, is involved at several key stages of cell division, and in particular is essential for cytokinesis in mammals (Hill et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hill et al., 2000.

claim: MKLP2 interacts with and is regulated by mitotic kinases including Cdk1/cyclin B prior to anaphase onset.
source: MKLP2 interacts with and is regulated by a number of mitotic kinases including Cdk1/cyclin B prior to anaphase onset (Hümmer and Mayer, 2009; Kitagawa et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hümmer and Mayer, 2009 and Kitagawa et al., 2014.

claim: MKLP2 is required for localisation of Chromosome Passenger Complex (CPC) components, including Aurora B kinase, to the midzone at anaphase.
source: MKLP2 is required for localisation of Chromosome Passenger Complex (CPC) components, including Aurora B kinase, to the midzone at anaphase (Gruneberg et al., 2004), which is in turn required for Kif4A and PRC1 function (Nunes Bastos et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gruneberg et al., 2004 and Nunes Bastos et al., 2013.

claim: MKLP2 participates in myosin II recruitment for cleavage furrow ingression.
source: MKLP2 also participates in myosin II recruitment for cleavage furrow ingression (Kitagawa et al., 2013) and interacts with the cell membrane to promote abscission (Fung et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kitagawa et al., 2013.

claim: MKLP2 interacts with the cell membrane to promote abscission.
source: MKLP2 also participates in myosin II recruitment for cleavage furrow ingression (Kitagawa et al., 2013) and interacts with the cell membrane to promote abscission (Fung et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fung et al., 2017.

claim: MKLP2 is a substrate for polo-like kinase 1 (Plk1), and the co-association at the midzone of MKLP2 and Plk1 is required for cytokinesis.
source: In addition, it is a substrate for polo-like kinase 1 (Plk1), and the co-association at the midzone of MKLP2 and Plk1 is also required for cytokinesis (Neef et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Neef et al., 2003.

claim: MKLP2 is found to be highly expressed in tumour tissue.
source: In the light of these activities and because MKLP2 is found to be highly expressed in tumour tissue (Gasnereau et al., 2012), inhibition of MKLP2 by antimitotics has been explored, and small molecule inhibitors of MKLP2 have been shown to perturb mammalian cytokinesis (Tcherniuk et al., 2010; Labrière et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gasnereau et al., 2012.

claim: Small molecule inhibitors of MKLP2 have been shown to perturb mammalian cytokinesis.
source: In the light of these activities and because MKLP2 is found to be highly expressed in tumour tissue (Gasnereau et al., 2012), inhibition of MKLP2 by antimitotics has been explored, and small molecule inhibitors of MKLP2 have been shown to perturb mammalian cytokinesis (Tcherniuk et al., 2010; Labrière et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tcherniuk et al., 2010 and Labrière et al., 2016.

claim: MKLP2 shares only approximately 35% sequence identity with kinesin-1.
source: MKLP2 shares only approximately 35% sequence identity with kinesin-1 (Kin1), which suggests that much of what is known about kinesin molecular function may not necessarily apply to this motor (Hizlan et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hizlan et al., 2006.

claim: The kinesin-6 MKLP1 is a plus-end directed motor.
source: A related kinesin family member, the kinesin-6 MKLP1 - part of the centralspindlin complex that is also essential for cytokinesis - is a plus-end directed motor (Nislow et al., 1992), as is Kif20B, another kinesin-6 (Abaza et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nislow et al., 1992.

claim: Kif20B, another kinesin-6, is a plus-end directed motor.
source: A related kinesin family member, the kinesin-6 MKLP1 - part of the centralspindlin complex that is also essential for cytokinesis - is a plus-end directed motor (Nislow et al., 1992), as is Kif20B, another kinesin-6 (Abaza et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Abaza et al., 2003.

claim: The centralspindlin holocomplex has anti-parallel microtubule (MT) bundling capability.
source: The centralspindlin holocomplex has anti-parallel microtubule (MT) bundling capability (Davies et al., 2015) consistent with its localisation and function in the spindle midzone.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Davies et al., 2015.

claim: Kinesin-6s are up to ~40% larger than the canonical Kin1 motor domain due to a number of unique loop insertions.
source: Kinesin-6s are particularly intriguing in this context because they are up to ~40% larger than the canonical Kin1 motor domain (Figure 1A) due to a number of unique loop insertions.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A showing domain organization.

claim: The mammalian MKLP2 motor domain contains a ~ 60 residue N-terminal extension, insertions in loop 2 (18 aa), loop 6 (99 aa), loop 8 (5 aa) and loop 12 (6 aa), along with an extended non-canonical neck-linker.
source: Within the mammalian MKLP2 motor domain sequence, these unique features include a ~ 60 residue N-terminal extension, insertions in loop 2 (18 aa), loop 6 (99 aa), loop 8 (5 aa) and loop 12 (6 aa), along with an extended non-canonical neck-linker; there is also a ~ 40 aa insert between this neck linker region and MKLP2's coiled coil.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing MKLP2 motor domain features.

claim: MKLP2 has a ~ 40 aa insert between the neck linker region and MKLP2's coiled coil.
source: Within the mammalian MKLP2 motor domain sequence, these unique features include a ~ 60 residue N-terminal extension, insertions in loop 2 (18 aa), loop 6 (99 aa), loop 8 (5 aa) and loop 12 (6 aa), along with an extended non-canonical neck-linker; there is also a ~ 40 aa insert between this neck linker region and MKLP2's coiled coil.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing MKLP2 motor domain features.

claim: MKLP2-MD (25-520) has a kcat of 4.38 ± 0.20 s−1 and K0.5,MT of 1.07 ± 0.18 μM.
source: Fits of the data to a Michaelis Menten function reveal values of kcat = 4.34 ± 0.14 s−1 and K0.5,MT = 0.93 ± 0.12μM for 1–520 and kcat = 4.38 ± 0.20 s−1 and K0.5,MT = 1.07 ± 0.18μM for 25–520, showing that the presence or absence of the extended MKLP2 N-terminus does not affect steady state ATPase parameters.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and described in the text.

claim: The presence or absence of the extended MKLP2 N-terminus (residues 1-25) does not affect steady state ATPase parameters.
source: Fits of the data to a Michaelis Menten function reveal values of kcat = 4.34 ± 0.14 s−1 and K0.5,MT = 0.93 ± 0.12μM for 1–520 and kcat = 4.38 ± 0.20 s−1 and K0.5,MT = 1.07 ± 0.18μM for 25–520, showing that the presence or absence of the extended MKLP2 N-terminus does not affect steady state ATPase parameters.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data for two constructs shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MT binding stimulates MKLP2 kcat >1000 fold.
source: MT binding stimulates kcat >1000 fold (Woehlke et al., 1997; Hackney, 1988; Gilbert et al., 1995) to levels similar to the mitotic kinesin-5 (Kin5) and about 10-fold slower than the transport kinesins Kin1 or Kin3 (Cochran et al., 2004) (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Woehlke et al., 1997; Hackney, 1988; Gilbert et al., 1995.

claim: MKLP2 kcat is similar to the mitotic kinesin-5 (Kin5) and about 10-fold slower than the transport kinesins Kin1 or Kin3.
source: MT binding stimulates kcat >1000 fold (Woehlke et al., 1997; Hackney, 1988; Gilbert et al., 1995) to levels similar to the mitotic kinesin-5 (Kin5) and about 10-fold slower than the transport kinesins Kin1 or Kin3 (Cochran et al., 2004) (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cochran et al., 2004 and comparison data in Table 1.

claim: The kinetics of binding 2'dmT to MKLP2-MD are essentially independent of MTs.
source: For 2'dmT (Figure 1C), rates in the presence and absence of MT are nearly identical (including Y intercept), implying that – unlike e.g. Kin-1 or Kin-5 – the kinetics of binding 2'dmT to MKLP2-MD are essentially independent of MTs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The rate of ADP release from MKLP2-MD in the absence of MTs is 51.9 ± 0.1 s−1.
source: Figure 1—figure supplement1 shows that the resulting fluorescence decrease, which reflects 2'dmD dissociation, fits a single exponential process with rate constant of 51.9 ± 0.1 s−1, i.e. the rate of ADP release from MKLP2-MD in the absence of MTs is unusually high.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rate of ADP release from MKLP2-MD in the absence of MTs is unusually high.
source: Figure 1—figure supplement1 shows that the resulting fluorescence decrease, which reflects 2'dmD dissociation, fits a single exponential process with rate constant of 51.9 ± 0.1 s−1, i.e. the rate of ADP release from MKLP2-MD in the absence of MTs is unusually high.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and comparison to other kinesins.

claim: There is a relative uncoupling of allosteric communication between the MT binding and catalytic sites in MKLP2-MD compared to other kinesins.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that there is a relative uncoupling of allosteric communication between the MT binding and catalytic sites in MKLP2-MD compared to other kinesins that have been described (Cochran et al., 2004; Ma and Taylor, 1995).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data and is supported by citations to Cochran et al., 2004 and Ma and Taylor, 1995.

claim: MT affinity of MKLP2-MD is modulated by the state of the catalytic site, with binding in the absence of nucleotide (NN) or presence of AMPPNP demonstrating a higher affinity than that with ADP or ADP.AlFx.
source: Like other kinesin family members (Table 1) (Atherton et al., 2014; Cochran et al., 2004; Rosenfeld et al., 1996; Nitta et al., 2004; Gigant et al., 2013; Cochran et al., 2006), MT affinity of MKLP2-MD is modulated by the state of the catalytic site, with binding in the absence of nucleotide (NN) or presence of AMPPNP demonstrating a higher affinity than that with ADP or ADP.AlFx (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Table 1, and citations to other kinesin studies.

claim: The ADP state of MKLP2-MD demonstrates a relatively high affinity for MTs.
source: In marked contrast to other kinesins, however, the ADP state of MKLP2-MD - which usually represents the kinesin weak binding state (Rosenfeld et al., 1996; Gigant et al., 2013; Crevel et al., 1996) – demonstrates a relatively high affinity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and citations to Rosenfeld et al., 1996; Gigant et al., 2013; Crevel et al., 1996.

claim: The difference in affinity between nucleotide states that in other kinesins are 'strong' binding (NN, AMPPNP) and 'weak' binding (ADP) is only about 8.5-fold for MKLP2-MD.
source: Thus, the difference in affinity between nucleotide states that in other kinesins are 'strong' binding (NN, AMPPNP) and 'weak' binding (ADP) is only about 8.5-fold.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: MKLP2-MD associates with MTs relatively strongly throughout its ATPase cycle.
source: Overall, MKLP2-MD associates with MTs relatively strongly throughout its ATPase cycle.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data on MT binding affinities.

claim: The overall organisation of MKLP2-MD is similar compared to other kinesins, with the major contact site between motor and MT being centred over the tubulin intradimer interface.
source: These structures show that the overall organisation of MKLP2-MD is similar compared to other kinesins, with the major contact site between motor and MT being centred over the tubulin intradimer interface (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The overall features of nucleotide-dependent subdomain movement described for Kin1 also apply to MKLP2.
source: Our reconstructions demonstrate that the overall features of nucleotide-dependent subdomain movement described for Kin1 also apply to MKLP2 (Figure 2D; Video 1), albeit the comparison is incomplete given the lack of a tubulin/MT-bound Kin1 ADP structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2D and Video 1.

claim: In the transition from ADP-bound to NN structures, the MKLP2 Switch I/II and P-loop subdomains both rotate away from each other slightly and relative to the static tubulin-binding domain.
source: In the transition from ADP-bound to NN structures (Figure 2D, left to middle), the MKLP2 Switch I/II and P-loop subdomains both rotate away from each other slightly and relative to the static tubulin-binding domain.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the transition from the NN to ADP.AlFx conformations, both the Switch I/II and P-loop subdomains rotate towards the catalytic site, with the rotation of the P-loop subdomain being greater than the Switch I/II subdomain.
source: In the transition from the NN to ADP.AlFx conformations (Figure 2D, middle to right), both domains rotate towards the catalytic site, with the rotation of the P-loop subdomain being greater than the Switch I/II subdomain.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Subdomain movements are a conserved facet of kinesin mechanochemistry even amongst motors with highly distinct functions.
source: This supports the idea that these subdomain movements are a conserved facet of kinesin mechanochemistry even amongst motors with highly distinct functions.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data comparing MKLP2 to other kinesins.

claim: In the MKLP2-MD-ADP structure, density corresponding to ADP is coordinated primarily via the P-loop with some connectivity to Switch II/loop11.
source: The properties of MKLP2-MD are such that an MT-bound MKLP2-MD-ADP structure could be captured, in which density corresponding to ADP is coordinated primarily via the P-loop with some connectivity to Switch II/loop11 (Figure 3, left; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In MT-bound MKLP2-MD-ADP, loop9 as well as the N-terminus of helix-α4 are more flexible compared to other kinesin-ADP conformations.
source: However, in MT-bound MKLP2-MD-ADP, loop9 as well as the N-terminus of helix-α4 are more flexible compared to these other kinesin-ADP conformations, reflecting distinct properties of MKLP2-MD.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data and comparison to other kinesins.

claim: In the MKLP2-MD-NN structure, no major conformational differences are seen compared to MKLP2-MD-ADP.
source: Highly unusually, in the MKLP2-MD-NN structure, no major conformational differences are seen compared to MKLP2-MD-ADP (Figure 3, middle), although nucleotide density is clearly lacking from the active site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The overall disordered nature of the N-terminus of helix-α4, loop 11 and loop 9 in MKLP2-MD-NN is very different from the more ordered conformation of these elements consistently seen in the MT-bound NN state of other plus-end kinesins.
source: The overall disordered nature of the N-terminus of helix-α4, loop 11 and loop 9 is very different from the more ordered conformation of these elements consistently seen in the MT-bound NN state of other plus-end kinesins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)(Atherton et al., 2014; Shang et al., 2014; Cao et al., 2014; Goulet et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to other kinesin studies.

claim: The MKLP2-MD-ADP and –NN structures are more similar to each other with respect to flexibility of MT binding elements at the helix-α4 N-terminus and loop11 than is typical for other kinesins.
source: Thus, the MKLP2-MD-ADP and –NN structures are more similar to each other with respect to flexibility of MT binding elements at the helix-α4 N-terminus and loop11 than is typical for other kinesins.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data comparing MKLP2 to other kinesins.

claim: Transition to the MKLP2-MD-ADP.AlFx structure causes substantial local rearrangements in the vicinity of the active site.
source: Transition to the MKLP2-MD-ADP.AlFx structure causes substantial local rearrangements in the vicinity of the active site (Figure 3, right), which are in turn linked to large subdomain rearrangements compared to the ADP-to-NN transition (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 2D.

claim: In the presence of the ADP.Pi-like analogue, stable conformations for all components around the active site are observed in MKLP2-MD.
source: However, in the presence of the ADP.Pi-like analogue, stable conformations for all components around the active site are also observed: density corresponding to the N-terminal end of helix-α4 and loop11 are seen and exhibit connectivity to adjacent regions (Figure 3, right), while the N-terminus of loop11 runs past the P-loop, the γ-phosphate mimic, and is connected to helix-α4, (Figure 3, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The compactness of the ATPase site in MKLP2-MD-ADP.AlFx is consistent with adoption of a catalytically competent conformation.
source: Overall, the compactness of the ATPase site is consistent with adoption of a catalytically competent conformation (Parke et al., 2010), similar to that seen in other kinesins, highlighting mechanochemical conservation within the superfamily with respect to closure of the active site to enable ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data and citation to Parke et al., 2010.

claim: In Kin1 and Kin3, the motor conformation in the presence of AMPPNP and ADP.AlFx are essentially indistinguishable.
source: In Kin1 and Kin3, the motor conformation in the presence of AMPPNP and ADP.AlFx are essentially indistinguishable (Atherton et al., 2014; Gigant et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Atherton et al., 2014 and Gigant et al., 2013.

claim: In MKLP2-MD, the AMPPNP reconstruction exhibits a similar conformation to the MKLP2-ADP and –NN reconstructions.
source: However, in MKLP2-MD, while density corresponding to bound AMPPNP is observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), none of the characteristic features in the motor observed for the catalytically competent ADP.AlFx conformation are seen upon AMPPNP binding. Instead, this reconstruction exhibits a similar conformation to the MKLP2-ADP and –NN reconstructions, such that at the nucleotide binding site, helix-α4 shows a partially extended conformation and only some density corresponding to loop9 and loop11 is visible (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The MKLP2-MD-AMPPNP reconstruction illustrates a large difference in structural response of MKLP2-MD to different ATP-like analogues - AMPPNP compared to ADP.AlFx.
source: This reconstruction thereby illustrates the large difference in structural response of MKLP2-MD to different ATP-like analogues - AMPPNP compared to ADP.AlFx – and is a further readout of the divergent properties of MKLP2.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data comparing MKLP2 responses to different nucleotides.

claim: The MKLP2-MD interface with the MT is composed of nucleotide-invariant and nucleotide-sensitive elements.
source: The MKLP2-MD interface with the MT is composed of nucleotide-invariant and nucleotide-sensitive elements.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: A 5 aa insertion in MKLP2-MD both contributes an additional helical turn to the C-terminus of helix-α4 and adds length to loop12 compared to Kin1.
source: In this subdomain of MKLP2-MD, a 5 aa insertion (Figure 2A) both contributes an additional helical turn to the C-terminus of helix-α4 and adds length to loop12 compared to Kin1 (Figure 4A); however this insert does not contact the MT.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 4A.

claim: The loop12 insert in MKLP2-MD does not contact the MT.
source: In this subdomain of MKLP2-MD, a 5 aa insertion (Figure 2A) both contributes an additional helical turn to the C-terminus of helix-α4 and adds length to loop12 compared to Kin1 (Figure 4A); however this insert does not contact the MT.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The C-terminus extension of helix-α4 in MKLP2-MD is nucleotide-insensitive.
source: This C-terminus extension of helix-α4 is nucleotide-insensitive (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,D) and thus is structurally similar to the helix-α4 extension formed by part of Kin3's loop12 insert (Atherton et al., 2014), although these insertions have no sequence homology.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,D and citation to Atherton et al., 2014.

claim: MKLP2-MD subdomain rearrangement in response to nucleotide causes nucleotide-dependent conformational changes in other elements at the MT binding interface.
source: MKLP2-MD subdomain rearrangement in response to nucleotide (Figure 2D) causes nucleotide-dependent conformational changes in other elements at the MT binding interface.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: MKLP2-MD's Switch I/II subdomain contains a 5 aa insertion in loop8, which is only well ordered in the presence of ADP.AlFx, and reaches across to contact H10-β9 of the neighbouring protofilament within the MT.
source: MKLP2's Switch I/II subdomain also contains a 5 aa insertion in loop8 (Figure 2A), which is only well ordered in the presence of ADP.AlFx, and reaches across to contact H10-β9 of the neighbouring protofilament within the MT (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2A, Figure 4B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,E.

claim: MKLP2-MD is the first kinesin described where a monomeric motor domain can bridge across two protofilaments.
source: To our knowledge MKLP2-MD is the first kinesin described where a monomeric motor domain can bridge across two protofilaments.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data and knowledge of other kinesins.

claim: MKLP2-MD has a larger 18 aa insert in both the β-sheet1 and loop2 of the P-loop subdomain.
source: MKLP2-MD also has a larger 18 aa insert (Figure 2A) in both the β-sheet1 and loop2 of the P-loop subdomain.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the NN and ADP states, density for the loop2 insert is not visible unless much less conservative thresholds are used, indicating greater flexibility of loop2 in these two states.
source: In the NN and ADP states, density for this insert is not visible unless much less conservative thresholds are used, indicating greater flexibility of loop2 in these two states (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,F.

claim: In the presence of ADP.AlFx, density for the loop2 element extends from the minus end of the MKLP2-MD and connects to α-tubulin.
source: In the presence of ADP.AlFx, density for this element extends from the minus end of the MKLP2-MD and connects to α-tubulin (Figure 4C), consistent with the large rotation of the P-loop subdomain in this ADP.AlFx state (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 2D.

claim: Compared to Kin1, the precise position and orientation of MKLP2-MD as a whole is noticeably shifted and rotated on the MT surface.
source: Compared to Kin1, not only does the MKLP2-MD contain extra sequences that contact the MT, but the precise position and orientation of MKLP2-MD as a whole is also noticeably shifted and rotated on the MT surface (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The shift and rotation of MKLP2-MD on the MT surface is present in both MT-bound NN and ADP.AlFx MKLP2-MD reconstructions, and is therefore independent of the nucleotide-dependent conformational changes.
source: A similar shift and rotation is present in both our MT-bound NN and ADP.AlFx MKLP2-MD reconstructions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and is therefore independent of the nucleotide-dependent conformational changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In MKLP2-MD, loop7 is closer to β-tubulin compared to Kin1.
source: For example, in MKLP2-MD, loop7 is closer to β-tubulin (Figure 4E) compared to Kin1, while the ordered single-turn helix in loop11 is closer to H3 than H12 in α-tubulin in the MKLP2-MD-ADP.AlFx state (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The ordered single-turn helix in loop11 is closer to H3 than H12 in α-tubulin in the MKLP2-MD-ADP.AlFx state.
source: For example, in MKLP2-MD, loop7 is closer to β-tubulin (Figure 4E) compared to Kin1, while the ordered single-turn helix in loop11 is closer to H3 than H12 in α-tubulin in the MKLP2-MD-ADP.AlFx state (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The collective effect of MKLP2-specific modifications leads to the shift and rotation of the MKLP2-MD on the MT surface.
source: Altogether, both kinesin-conserved and MKLP2-MD-specific elements contribute to the motor's interaction with the MT, several of which are nucleotide sensitive. The collective effect of MKLP2-specific modifications leads to the shift and rotation of the MKLP2-MD on the MT surface.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: The differences in MKLP-MD compared to Kin1 modify its footprint on the MT surface, leading to MKLP2-MD contacting a greater MT surface area in all states.
source: The differences in MKLP-MD compared to Kin1 also modify its footprint on the MT surface, leading to MKLP2-MD contacting a greater MT surface area in all states (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The enhancing effect of the shift and rotation is most clearly seen in the increased footprint of loop7 and α4 (in both NN and ADP.AlFx states), and loop11 in the ADP.AlFx state.
source: The enhancing effect of the shift and rotation (Figure 4D) is most clearly seen in the increased footprint of loop7 and α4 (in both NN and ADP.AlFx states), and loop11 in the ADP.AlFx state (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4D, Figure 5, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The transition from NN to ADP.AlFx states brings loop7 and loop8 into more extensive contact with β-tubulin's H4.
source: The transition from NN to ADP.AlFx states and further rotation of the Switch I/II subdomain brings loop7 and loop8 into even more extensive contact with β-tubulin's H4, while full ordering of helix-α4 and loop11 adjacent to the active site leads to additional contacts with α-tubulin.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: Full ordering of helix-α4 and loop11 adjacent to the active site leads to additional contacts with α-tubulin.
source: The transition from NN to ADP.AlFx states and further rotation of the Switch I/II subdomain brings loop7 and loop8 into even more extensive contact with β-tubulin's H4, while full ordering of helix-α4 and loop11 adjacent to the active site leads to additional contacts with α-tubulin.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: Ordering of MKLP2-specfic insertions that are present in the ADP.AlFx reconstruction produce a further enhancement of the MKLP2-MD footprint.
source: Moreover, ordering of MKLP2-specfic insertions that are present in the ADP.AlFx reconstruction produce a further enhancement of the MKLP2-MD footprint (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The electrostatic surface of MKLP2-MD shows a more pronounced positive interaction surface compared to kinesin-1, especially around the C-terminal end of helix-α4.
source: In addition to the enlarged footprint of MKLP2-MD on the negatively charged MT surface (Woehlke et al., 1997), the electrostatic surface of MKLP2-MD shows a more pronounced positive interaction surface compared to kinesin-1, especially around the C-terminal end of helix-α4, a region that is nucleotide invariant.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data and citation to Woehlke et al., 1997.

claim: Through its ATPase cycle, the footprint of MKLP2-MD on the MT is altered and is most different in its ATP-like state.
source: Thus, through its ATPase cycle, the footprint of MKLP2-MD on the MT is altered and is most different in its ATP-like state.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: Nucleotide-dependent subdomain rearrangements in MKLP2-MD yield conformational changes at both termini of the motor.
source: Nucleotide-dependent subdomain rearrangements in MKLP2-MD yield conformational changes at both termini of the motor.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: With ADP bound, the C-terminal helix-α6 lies close to the motor-MT interface and terminates adjacent to the C-terminus of helix-α4.
source: With ADP bound, as for other kinesins, the C-terminal helix-α6 lies close to the motor-MT interface and terminates adjacent to the C-terminus of helix-α4 (Figure 6A, arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The density for helix-α6 in MKLP2-MD-ADP is less well-defined, with a length of three helical turns at most and is thus shorter than typically seen in other kinesins.
source: The density for helix-α6 is less well-defined, with a length of three helical turns at most and is thus shorter than typically seen in other kinesins (Figure 6A, arrowhead; [Atherton et al., 2014; Shang et al., 2014]).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 6A and citations to Atherton et al., 2014 and Shang et al., 2014.

claim: In the MKLP2-MD-ADP configuration, extension of helix-α6, docking of the neck-linker and formation of the cover-neck bundle (CNB) are all prevented.
source: In this configuration, extension of helix-α6, docking of the neck-linker and formation of the cover-neck bundle (CNB) are all prevented.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: In the NN reconstruction, the overall organisation of the neck-linker region is very similar to that in the ADP state.
source: In the NN reconstruction, the overall organisation of this region is very similar to that in the ADP state (Figure 6B) (and of the AMPPNP state, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), although density corresponding to helix-α6 is better defined in the NN compared to the ADP structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Following the subdomain rearrangement accompanying the NN/ADP.AlFx transition, the neck-linker cleft opens.
source: Following the subdomain rearrangement accompanying the NN/ADP.AlFx transition, the neck-linker cleft opens.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: Helix-α6 of MKLP2-MD extends beneath the core β-sheet in the ADP.AlFx state, thereby directing the neck-linker towards the MT plus end.
source: Helix-α6 of MKLP2-MD extends beneath the core β-sheet, thereby directing the neck-linker towards the MT plus end (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Anisotropy decay curves show that the MKLP2-MD neck-linker becomes more ordered in the presence of ADP.AlFx compared to the absence of nucleotide, and depends on MT binding.
source: In support of partial docking and reorientation of the neck-linker, anisotropy decay curves show that the MKLP2-MD neck-linker becomes more ordered in the presence of ADP.AlFx - as shown by the increase in rotational correlation time - compared to the absence of nucleotide, and depends on MT binding (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Density corresponding to C-terminal residues extending from around H508, which would correspond to a docked neck-linker conformation, is not visible in the ADP.AlFx density map.
source: Strikingly, however, density corresponding to C-terminal residues extending from around H508, which would correspond to a docked neck-linker conformation, is not visible in the ADP.AlFx density map (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The neck-linker sequence of MKLP2 differs markedly from other plus-end kinesins.
source: Consistent with a non-canonical neck-linker conformation, the neck-linker sequence itself differs markedly from other plus-end kinesins (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In MKLP2, two conserved Asn residues that make hydrogen bonds against the core in other plus-end directed kinesins have been substituted for basic His residues, which would be predicted to preclude neck-linker docking.
source: Most plus-end directed kinesins have a conserved sequence in which two Asn residues make hydrogen bonds against the core, stabilizing neck-linker docking (Gigant et al., 2013) (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2). In MKLP2, these two Asn residues have been substituted for basic His residues, which would be predicted to preclude neck-linker docking.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and citation to Gigant et al., 2013.

claim: Conserved core residues contacting the neck-linker region in plus-end directed kinesins are not fully conserved in MKLP2.
source: In addition, conserved core residues contacting this region of the neck-linker in plus-end directed kinesins are not fully conserved in MKLP2; for example Kin1-Y77→MKLP2- Q151 (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Although subdomain rearrangement results in reorientation of the MKLP2-MD neck-linker towards the MT plus end, the docking of the neck linker that is typically seen does not occur in MKLP2-MD.
source: Thus, although subdomain rearrangement results in reorientation of the MKLP2-MD neck-linker towards the MT plus end – as with other plus end kinesins – the docking of the neck linker that is typically seen does not occur in MKLP2-MD.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: Loop6 is the largest MKLP2-specific insertion (99 aa) and density corresponding to it is present in all nucleotide states.
source: Loop6 is the largest MKLP2-specific insertion (99 aa) and density corresponding to it is present in all nucleotide states (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loop6 emerges from the side of the motor domain facing the MT plus end.
source: The higher resolution of the ADP.AlFx reconstruction facilitates the characterisation of density corresponding to loop6 (Figure 7A,B, Video 3), which emerges from the side of the motor domain facing the MT plus end.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7A,B and Video 3.

claim: Loop6 is effectively part of the SwI/II subdomain.
source: Given its position, connectivity and its apparent movement in the NN/ADP.AlFx transition, it is effectively part of the SwI/II subdomain (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Loop6 forms density that spreads across the MT-facing surface of the central β-sheet.
source: Loop6 forms density that spreads across the MT-facing surface of the central β-sheet.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data.

claim: Loop6 density connects the MT facing surface of the core β-sheet with β-sheet-5a/b of the tubulin-binding subdomain that connects to the MT surface.
source: This density also connects the MT facing surface of the core β-sheet with β-sheet-5a/b of the tubulin-binding subdomain that connects to the MT surface (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Loop6 itself does not appear to contact the MT surface.
source: However, loop6 itself does not appear to contact the MT surface.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: Secondary structure prediction of loop6 converged on the presence of a 4-turn helical region towards its N-terminus.
source: Creating a full model of loop6 was not possible, but secondary structure prediction of loop6 converged on the presence of a 4-turn helical region towards its N-terminus (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by secondary structure prediction data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Density that corresponds to a helical structure was observed lying close to helix-α3 in loop6.
source: Density that corresponds to a helical structure was observed lying close to helix-α3 and we modelled an α-helix within it (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: The rest of loop6 has no predicted secondary structure and may be intrinsically disordered.
source: However, the rest of loop6 has no predicted secondary structure and may be intrinsically disordered (Seeger and Rice, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by secondary structure prediction and citation to Seeger and Rice, 2013.

claim: Loop6 is incompletely visualised, partly due to the lack of discrete secondary structural elements and also presumably due to flexibility in this region of the motor.
source: As displayed in Figure 7A,B, loop6 is incompletely visualised, partly due to the lack of discrete secondary structural elements and also presumably due to flexibility in this region of the motor.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: With coarser (low-pass) filtering of the EM reconstruction, a large and lower resolution cloud of density is revealed for loop6.
source: This conclusion is reinforced when, with coarser (low-pass) filtering of the EM reconstruction, a large and lower resolution cloud of density is revealed (Figure 7D), consistent with what was previously described from a 2.5 nm resolution reconstruction of the C. elegans kinesin-6, MKLP1 (Zen4) (Hizlan et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7D and citation to Hizlan et al., 2006.

claim: The large and lower resolution cloud of density for loop6 is unconnected to other regions of the motor domain, and does not contact adjacent motor domains or the MT, but likely corresponds to multiple flexible conformations of the remaining loop6 residues.
source: This density is unconnected to other regions of the motor domain, and does not contact adjacent motor domains or the MT, but likely corresponds to multiple flexible conformations of the remaining loop6 residues.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: The nucleotide-dependent movement of three conserved, mobile elements at the junction of the three subdomains can be tracked: the P-loop, loop9, and loop 11.
source: At the MKLP2-MD catalytic site, the nucleotide-dependent movement of three conserved, mobile elements that lie at the junction of the three subdomains can be tracked: (1) the P-loop (brown); (2) loop9 (yellow, contains Switch I); (3) loop 11 (red, contains Switch II) (Figure 3, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3 and Video 2.

claim: The N-terminal half of helix-α4 lies at the back of the nucleotide-binding site and provides a structural link to the MT binding interface.
source: The N-terminal half of helix-α4 lies at the back of the nucleotide-binding site and provides a structural link to the MT binding interface.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: The P-loop, loop9, and loop11 are sensors of the nucleotide present in the active site and also participate in the conformational response of the motor domain to nucleotide.
source: These elements are sensors of the nucleotide present in the active site and also participate in the conformational response of the motor domain to nucleotide.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of kinesin mechanochemistry.

claim: MKLP2 follows the same state-dependent sequence of changes at the NC and PC clefts as Kin1.
source: MKLP2 follows the same state-dependent sequence of changes at the NC and PC clefts as Kin1.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data comparing MKLP2 to Kin1.

claim: For MKLP2-MD in the ADP-bound structure, the PC is open, while the NC is closed and the DC for the neck-linker is also closed.
source: Thus, for MKLP2-MD: (i) in the ADP-bound structure, the PC is open, while the NC is closed and the DC for the neck-linker is also closed;
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: For MKLP2-MD in the NN state, the PC is closed while the NC is open, such that the DC remains closed.
source: (ii) in the NN state, the PC is closed while the NC is open, such that the DC remains closed;
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: For MKLP2-MD in the ADP.AlFx state in which the active site is closed in a catalytic-competent conformation, both the PC and NC are closed leading to an opening of the DC and reorientation of the neck-linker towards the MT plus end.
source: (iii) in the ADP.AlFx state in which the active site is closed in a catalytic-competent conformation, both the PC and NC are closed leading to an opening of the DC and reorientation of the neck-linker towards the MT plus end.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: MKLP2-MD structures reinforce the logic of cleft opening/closure with respect to kinesin mechanochemistry first described for Kin1, while demonstrating an elaboration of motor function through family-specific modifications.
source: Our MKLP2-MD structures thus reinforce the logic of cleft opening/closure with respect to kinesin mechanochemistry first described for Kin1 (Shang et al., 2014), while demonstrating an elaboration of motor function through family-specific modifications.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data and citation to Shang et al., 2014.

claim: The kcat of MKLP2-MD (4.4 s−1) is ~10 fold lower than kinesin-1 and -3.
source: The kcat of MKLP2-MD (4.4 s−1) is ~10 fold lower than kinesin-1 and -3 (Table 1) and a number of MKLP2-MD substitutions at otherwise highly conserved regions could influence multiple steps in its catalytic cycle.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: MKLP2-MD has low ADP affinity in solution and this is barely altered on interaction with MTs.
source: For example, MKLP2-MD has low ADP affinity in solution and this is barely altered on interaction with MTs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The ADP release rate in the absence of MTs for MKLP2-MD is only 2–3-fold less than that for Kin1/3 s in the presence of saturating MTs.
source: Indeed, the ADP release rate in the absence of MTs is only 2–3-fold less than that for Kin1/3 s in the presence of saturating MTs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and comparison to other kinesins.

claim: While MT binding activates the MKLP2 ATPase, its basal ADP release rate is higher than kcat.
source: Thus, while MT binding activates the MKLP2 ATPase, its basal ADP release rate is higher than kcat.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The small structural changes observed when comparing MKLP2 ADP and NN structures is a distinctive property of these MKLP2/MT complexes compared to other plus end kinesins.
source: The small structural changes observed when comparing our ADP and NN structures – in particular, that the N-terminus of helix-α4 and loop11 remain largely disordered in the NN state – is a distinctive property of these MKLP2/MT complexes compared to other plus end kinesins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 [Atherton et al., 2014; Shang et al., 2014; Goulet et al., 2014; Cao et al., 2014]).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to other kinesin studies.

claim: Substitutions at conserved sites around the nucleotide pocket might be predicted to destabilise the nucleotide binding network that is present in other kinesins.
source: Substitutions at conserved sites around the nucleotide pocket might be predicted to destabilise the nucleotide binding network that is present in other kinesins.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on sequence analysis and structural data.

claim: The collective effect of substitutions in MKLP2-MD is likely to be the reason for lower stabilisation of nucleotide binding to MKLP2-MD.
source: We conclude that the collective effect of these substitutions – along with possible effects from the shift of MKLP2-MD binding on the MT surface – is likely to be the reason for lower stabilisation of nucleotide binding to MKLP2-MD.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Previously proposed mechanisms of MT-stimulated ADP release in Kin1/3 s may not be applicable to MKLP2-MD.
source: Therefore, previously proposed mechanisms of MT-stimulated ADP release in Kin1/3 s may not be applicable to MKLP2-MD (Atherton et al., 2014; Shang et al., 2014; Cao et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the biochemical and structural data, and citations to other kinesin studies.

claim: The structure of the MKLP2-MD-ADP.AlFx reconstruction suggests that MT binding participates in stabilising helix-α4 and loop11 in this structure.
source: The structure of the MKLP2-MD-ADP.AlFx reconstruction suggests that MT binding participates in stabilising helix-α4 and loop11 in this structure, supporting the conserved SwitchI/II and P-loop residues in adopting a catalytically relevant conformation.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: The MKLP2-ADP.AlFx reconstruction is overall comparable to hydrolysis-competent conformations seen in Kin1/3/4/5 with a so-called phosphate tube formed from loop9 and 11 supporting ATP hydrolysis.
source: The MKLP2-ADP.AlFx reconstruction is overall comparable to hydrolysis-competent conformations seen in Kin1/3/4/5 with a so-called phosphate tube formed from loop9 and 11 supporting ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data and comparison to other kinesins.

claim: The reconstruction in the presence of AMPPNP most closely resembles that of ADP – rather than ADP.AlFx as is seen in Kin1/3.
source: However, the reconstruction in the presence of AMPPNP most closely resembles that of ADP – rather than ADP.AlFx as is seen in Kin1/3 – and it may also represent the MKLP2-MD NN conformation after AMPPNP has bound to it.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: MKLP2-specific substitutions within and around the nucleotide binding site influence the binding kinetics and structural transitions of MT-bound MKLP2-MD in response to different nucleotides.
source: This too could be a reflection of MKLP2-specific substitutions within and around the nucleotide binding site (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) that influence the binding kinetics and structural transitions of MT-bound MKLP2-MD in response to different nucleotides, and which also contribute to the overall turnover rate of the motor's ATPase.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The MKLP2-MD steady state ATPase activity shows that its K0.5,MT is ~1.1 μM.
source: The MKLP2-MD steady state ATPase activity shows that its K0.5,MT is ~1.1 μM.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: While the affinity of MKLP2-MD for MTs is higher in the NN and AMPPNP states, there is less effect of nucleotide on the overall affinity of the MKLP2-MD for MTs compared to Kin1.
source: This agrees well with the co-sedimentation analysis, which also shows that, while the affinity is higher in the NN and AMPPNP states, there is less effect of nucleotide on the overall affinity of the MKLP2-MD for MTs compared to Kin1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The reconstructions do not provide obvious structural explanations for the subtle nucleotide-dependent differences in the MT affinity of MKLP2-MD.
source: Our reconstructions do not provide obvious structural explanations for these subtle nucleotide-dependent differences in the MT affinity of MKLP2-MD.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: It is possible that the flexible loops formed by the MKLP2-MD specific insertions do not directly contribute to differences in affinity in this motor compared to Kin1.
source: Indeed, the additional MKLP2-MD loop contacts with the MT were modelled most easily in the highest resolution reconstruction (ADP.AlFx), which has a slightly lower MT affinity. It is thus possible that the flexible loops formed by the MKLP2-MD specific insertions do not directly contribute to differences in affinity in this motor compared to Kin1; rather this is dominated by the differences in the surface charge of the MT interface (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the structural data shown in Figure 5.

claim: MKLP2-MD K0.5,MT is ~10 fold lower than the Kin1 motor domain (13 μM).
source: MKLP2-MD K0.5,MT is ~10 fold lower than the Kin1 motor domain (13 μM) (Atherton et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Atherton et al., 2014.

claim: The MKLP2-MD MT interface is overall more positively charged than that of Kin1, which likely contributes to the overall increased affinity of MKLP2 throughout the ATPase cycle.
source: While both motors bind MTs via their conserved tubulin-binding subdomains, strikingly the MKLP2-MD MT interface is overall more positively charged than that of Kin1, which likely contributes to the overall increased affinity of MKLP2 throughout the ATPase cycle.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: The MKLP2-specific, nucleotide invariant extension of loop12 is positively charged and may interact with the nearby acidic C-terminal tails (CTTs) of β-tubulin.
source: In addition, the MKLP2-specific, nucleotide invariant extension of loop12 is positively charged and may interact with the nearby acidic C-terminal tails (CTTs) of β-tubulin, although there is no visible connection in our reconstructions, likely due to its conformational variability.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the structural data.

claim: A similar interaction between the β-tubulin CTT and loop12 of Kin3 has previously been described.
source: A similar interaction between the β-tubulin CTT and loop12 of Kin3 has previously been described (Okada and Hirokawa, 2000), although Kin3 loop12 has a higher net positive charge (+4) than MKLP2 and is longer and conformationally flexible in all nucleotide states (Atherton et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Okada and Hirokawa, 2000 and Atherton et al., 2014.

claim: Sequence insertions within loop2 are more usually associated with depolymerisation activity, for example in Kin13s.
source: Sequence insertions within loop2 are more usually associated with depolymerisation activity, for example in Kin13s (Ogawa et al., 2004), but here MKLP2-MD loop2 appears to simply form a MT contact, with no current evidence of MKLP2 activity influencing MT dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ogawa et al., 2004 and inference from the structural data.

claim: MKLP2-MD loop2 appears to simply form a MT contact, with no current evidence of MKLP2 activity influencing MT dynamics.
source: Sequence insertions within loop2 are more usually associated with depolymerisation activity, for example in Kin13s (Ogawa et al., 2004), but here MKLP2-MD loop2 appears to simply form a MT contact, with no current evidence of MKLP2 activity influencing MT dynamics.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: MKLP2-MD altered position on the MT surface may regulate the transition rates between structural states.
source: Thus, while not sufficient to perturb the fundamentals of nucleotide-sensitive subdomain rearrangement or formation of a hydrolysis competent conformation at the active site, MKLP2-MD altered position on the MT surface may regulate the transition rates between structural states.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the structural data.

claim: The altered footprint of MKLP2-MD may enable MKLP2 to select different populations of MT tracks within the spindle for interaction.
source: The altered footprint may also enable MKLP2 to select different populations of MT tracks within the spindle for interaction.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the structural data.

claim: The structural characterisation of MKLP2-MD suggests that the binding site of kinesins on the MT surface has some previously unsuspected plasticity that enables tuning of motor function while still supporting conserved conformational changes.
source: Thus, our structural characterisation of MKLP2-MD suggests that the binding site of kinesins on the MT surface has some previously unsuspected plasticity that enables tuning of motor function while still supporting conserved conformational changes.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: In Kin1/3/5, the key conformational change elicited by ATP binding to MT-associated motors is ordering of the neck-linker towards the MT plus end.
source: In Kin1/3/5, the key conformational change elicited by ATP binding to MT-associated motors is ordering of the neck-linker towards the MT plus end (Rice et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rice et al., 1999.

claim: Neck-linker docking in Kin1/3/5 is supported by formation of the CNB between the neck-linker and the motor domain N-terminus.
source: Such neck-linker docking is supported by formation of the CNB between the neck-linker and the motor domain N-terminus (Khalil et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Khalil et al., 2008.

claim: In MKLP2, reorientation of the neck-linker and CNB formation occur in the presence of ADP.AlFx and the neck-linker is less mobile than in other nucleotide states.
source: In MKLP2, reorientation of the neck-linker and CNB formation occur in the presence of ADP.AlFx and the neck-linker is less mobile than in other nucleotide states (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: CNB formation in MKLP2 is consistent with conservation across all N-kinesins including MKLP2 of a cluster of hydrophobic residues in this region of the motor domain.
source: CNB formation is, however, consistent with conservation across all N-kinesins including MKLP2 of a cluster of hydrophobic residues in this region of the motor domain (Figure 6 [Hwang et al., 2008]).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 6 and citation to Hwang et al., 2008.

claim: Formation of the CNB contributes to stable closure of the nucleotide binding pocket and supports ATPase activity.
source: Formation of the CNB also contributes to stable closure of the nucleotide binding pocket and supports ATPase activity (Cao et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cao et al., 2014.

claim: The distal region of the putative MKLP2-MD neck-linker does not visibly dock along the plus end portion of the motor domain core, and demonstrates residual flexibility despite CNB formation.
source: Remarkably, however, the distal region of the putative MKLP2-MD neck-linker does not visibly dock along the plus end portion of the motor domain core, and demonstrates residual flexibility despite CNB formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data.

claim: The observation of non-docking neck-linker in MKLP2 is consistent with the divergent MKLP2 sequences both in the neck-linker and along the core β-sheet where the neck-linker might otherwise dock.
source: This observation is consistent with the divergent MKLP2 sequences both in the neck-linker and along the core β-sheet where the neck-linker might otherwise dock (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2) [Vale and Fletterick, 1997]).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and citation to Vale and Fletterick, 1997.

claim: The MKLP2-MD neck-linker contains two adjacent proline residues (P510 and P511) that are likely to affect the conformation of the neck-linker.
source: Furthermore, the MKLP2-MD neck-linker also contains two adjacent proline residues (P510 and P511) that are likely to affect the conformation of the neck-linker.
evidence: The claim is an inference from sequence data.

claim: Divergence in the distal neck-linker region is a feature of the MKLP2 sequence in a number of organisms.
source: Divergence in the distal neck-linker region is a feature of the MKLP2 sequence in a number of organisms (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The structural findings suggest that analysis of sequences immediately C-terminal of kinesin motor domains could be considered in two segments according to (1) CNB formation by the proximal region and (2) docking of the distal region, when predicting motor function.
source: Indeed, our structural findings suggest that analysis of sequences immediately C-terminal of kinesin motor domains could be considered in two segments according to (1) CNB formation by the proximal region and (2) docking of the distal region, when predicting motor function.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: It is not known if dimers of MKLP2 operate by taking steps in the same way as characterised for transport kinesins.
source: It is not known if dimers of MKLP2 operate by taking steps in the same way as characterised for transport kinesins, and our structures predict that the molecular properties of full length MKLP2 are likely to be distinct from Kin1.
evidence: The claim is a statement of current knowledge and an inference from the structural data.

claim: The MKLP2 neck region – separating the neck-linker and the coiled coil – is substantially longer (~40 residues) than for example Kin1, making it unlikely that conventional models of processive stepping apply to MKLP2.
source: In addition, the MKLP2 neck region – separating the neck-linker and the coiled coil – is substantially longer (~40 residues) than for example Kin1, making it unlikely that conventional models of processive stepping apply to MKLP2.
evidence: The claim is an inference from sequence data.

claim: The N-terminal helical portion of loop6 is likely to be conserved in MKLP2s in metazoa.
source: In addition, sequence analysis suggests that the N-terminal helical portion of loop6 is also likely to be conserved in MKLP2s in metazoa (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A structural snapshot of the C. elegans kinesin-6 Zen4 motor domain in the absence of its MT/tubulin track was published during preparation of the manuscript.
source: During preparation of our manuscript, a structural snapshot of the C. elegans kinesin-6 Zen4 motor domain in the absence of its MT/tubulin track was published (Guan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Guan et al., 2017.

claim: Although the loop6 insertion of Zen4 is substantially shorter than in MKLP2, a helical segment is also observed in this region of Zen4.
source: Intriguingly, although the loop6 insertion of this MKLP1 relative is substantially shorter than in MKLP2, a helical segment is also observed in this region of Zen4, consistent with our predictions.
evidence: The claim is an inference from comparison to the Zen4 structure.

claim: The connectivity of loop6 in MKLP2 and Zen4 is different, with MKLP2 loop6 forming much more extensive contacts with other regions within the SwI/II subdomain.
source: However, the connectivity of loop6 in the two kinesin-6s is different, with MKLP2 loop6 forming much more extensive contacts with other regions within the SwI/II subdomain.
evidence: The claim is an inference from comparison to the Zen4 structure.

claim: Loop6 could have an overall modulatory role on motor mechanochemistry.
source: This leaves open the question as to this loop's functional contribution to MKLP2. Given its connectivity with more conserved portions of the motor domain such as loop8/beta-5, it could have an overall modulatory role on motor mechanochemistry.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the structural data.

claim: Loop6 is possibly the binding site for other regulatory components of the central spindle.
source: It is also possible that it is the binding site for other regulatory components of the central spindle.
evidence: The claim is a speculation.

claim: Sequence comparisons informed by structural data suggest that the presence of loop6, other extended insertions including loop2, and modifications related to neck-linker docking are highly characteristic of the kinesin-6 subfamily of motors.
source: Sequence comparisons informed by our structural data suggest that the presence of loop6, other extended insertions including loop2, and modifications related to neck-linker docking are highly characteristic of this subfamily of motors.
evidence: The claim is an inference from sequence and structural data.

claim: The structural data could be used to predict the properties of other members of the kinesin-6 subfamily, including the two other kinesin-6 family members within vertebrates.
source: Thus, our structural data shed light on the unusual mechanochemistry of the MKLP2-MD and could be used to predict the properties of other members of the kinesin-6 subfamily, including the two other kinesin-6 family members within vertebrates.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: Sequence analysis in the structural context of one highly divergent kinesin subfamily can be mapped onto other members of the wider superfamily.
source: Similarly, sequence analysis in the structural context of one highly divergent kinesin subfamily can also be mapped onto other members of the wider superfamily.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the structural data.

claim: The structural and biophysical characterisations of the MKLP2 motor domain suggest that this protein and its relatives could act as an organiser or a tension sensor, rather than a classical transport motor, within the MT bundles at the spindle midzone.
source: Our structural and biophysical characterisations of the MKLP2 motor domain suggest that this protein and its relatives could act as an organiser or a tension sensor, rather than a classical transport motor, within the MT bundles at the spindle midzone.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the structural and biophysical data.

claim: A non-transport role for kinesin-6s was implied by recent computational analysis of the kinesin superfamily.
source: A non-transport role for kinesin-6s was also implied by recent computational analysis of the kinesin superfamily (Richard et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Richard et al., 2016.

claim: MKLP2 inhibitor studies highlight the importance of the ATPase activity of MKLP2 for its role within the spindle.
source: Nevertheless, MKLP2 inhibitor studies highlight the importance of the ATPase activity of MKLP2 for its role within the spindle, suggesting that the nucleotide-dependent conformational changes we have described are important for its mitotic function (Labrière et al., 2016).
